beginner: Sour cherry wants a deep, fertile soil that drains fast. Good drainage is the rule you cannot bend: cherry roots are very sensitive to wet feet and to the root and crown rots that follow soggy ground, and standing water also invites bacterial canker. A loam or sandy loam is ideal. Heavy clay that holds water is the trouble spot; if that is your soil, plant on a raised mound and choose a rootstock that tolerates heavier ground (Mazzard or Gisela 6). A near-neutral soil with some compost worked in suits it well.
seasoned: Sour cherry demands a deep, well-drained, fertile loam; drainage is the non-negotiable, since cherry roots will not tolerate wet feet and waterlogged ground brings on root and crown rot and predisposes the tree to bacterial canker. A loam or sandy loam is well suited; heavy, water-holding clay is the problem texture. On clay, plant on a raised berm and pair the tree with a heavier-soil-tolerant rootstock (Mazzard or a Gisela) rather than the drainage-fussy Mahaleb. Moderate fertility with modest organic matter is ideal.

beginner: Sour cherry grows best in a near-neutral soil, around pH 6.5 to 7.0, and is fine from about 6.0 to 7.5 (pH just measures how acidic or alkaline the soil is). Test your soil before planting and adjust slowly if needed: garden lime raises the pH if the soil is too acidic, and elemental sulfur lowers it if it is too alkaline. Mix any of this in before you plant, because pH changes slowly and is far easier to fix before the permanent tree goes in.
seasoned: Sour cherry does best in a near-neutral soil, roughly pH 6.5 to 7.0, and tolerates about 6.0 to 7.5. Test the soil before planting and adjust gradually if needed: lime raises a too-acidic pH, elemental sulfur lowers one that is too alkaline. Work amendments in ahead of planting, since pH shifts slowly and is far easier to correct before the permanent tree is in the ground.

beginner: Feed once in early spring before the tree starts growing. Scatter the fertilizer evenly on the soil around the tree out to where the branches reach, keep it off the trunk, and water it in. Sour cherry needs less feeding than peach, so go light: if the tree is making plenty of new growth, it may need none at all. Never feed late in the year, because soft late growth gets damaged by winter cold, and that damage is how the serious disease bacterial canker gets in.
seasoned: Feed lightly in early spring before growth begins, broadcasting evenly around the root zone out to the drip line, off the trunk, and watering it in. Sour cherry needs less nitrogen than peach: aim for about 8 to 12 inches of new shoot growth a year on a bearing tree, and ease off if it makes more. Never feed late in the season, since late nitrogen pushes soft growth that winter cold injures, and that injury is the main entry point for bacterial canker.

beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) works for backyard cherries, used sparingly. Do not overdo nitrogen, the first number, because too much pushes leafy growth that is more prone to disease and winter damage.
seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 suits backyard cherries, applied modestly. Avoid high-nitrogen feeding, which drives soft, canker-prone, overly vigorous growth at the expense of fruiting and winter hardiness.

beginner: A simple guide is a small handful of 10-10-10 for each year of the tree's age, up to a modest amount, spread once in early spring before the buds open. Do not put fertilizer in the planting hole or feed right at planting; wait until the tree starts growing. If the tree is already growing a foot of new branch each year, it probably needs no feeding at all.
seasoned: A common home rate is about 1/8 pound of actual nitrogen per year of tree age, to a modest maximum, applied once in early spring before bud break, scaled DOWN from peach rates because cherry is canker-prone under heavy nitrogen. Do not fertilize at planting or place fertilizer in the hole; wait until growth begins. Judge by shoot growth: a bearing tree wants only 8 to 12 inches of new wood a year.

beginner: A sour cherry does not need a companion tree to pollinate it, since it fruits on its own. What matters for a tree is the ground around the roots, not the usual vegetable partners: keep grass and weeds pulled back from under the branches, because lawn competes hard with a young tree, and a mulched, weed-free area helps it settle in. Flowers that bring in bees can help the short bloom set well. The one site rule is replant disease: do not plant a cherry where a cherry, plum, peach, or apricot was recently growing.
seasoned: Because sour cherry is self-fruitful, it needs no companion pollinizer, unlike sweet cherry. The interactions that matter for a tree are at the root zone, not classic vegetable pairings: keep turf and weeds cleared back from under the canopy, since they compete hard with a young tree, and a mulched, competition-free root area establishes it faster. A skirt of pollinator plants can lift bee activity at the short bloom. The one site rule is replant disease: do not follow stone fruit with stone fruit on the same ground.

beginner: Cherries that look normal on the outside but have a small white maggot (a grub) inside, near the pit, with brown mushy flesh around it. You often do not see it until you cut or bite one. It starts as the fruit begins to color.
seasoned: Cherries that look fine outside but hide a small white maggot inside, near the pit, with the flesh browning around it. Infested fruit softens and may show a tiny egg-laying dimple; damage worsens as the fruit colors toward harvest.

beginner: Small flies called cherry fruit flies. They spend winter in the soil, come out in late spring, and lay eggs under the skin of cherries once they start to color. The eggs hatch into the maggots you find inside. There is just one round a year, and green fruit is safe, so the danger starts at color change.
seasoned: Cherry fruit flies, chiefly the eastern cherry fruit fly (Rhagoletis cingulata) and black cherry fruit fly (R. fausta) across the sour cherry belt, and the western cherry fruit fly (R. indifferens) in the West. Pupae overwinter in the soil; adults emerge in late spring, and after a short maturation the females lay eggs just under the skin of coloring fruit. One generation a year, and green fruit is safe, so timing tracks the color change.

beginner: Once the maggots are inside, no spray reaches them. The fixes are cleanup and timing: pick every cherry promptly, pick up and destroy fallen fruit so the grubs cannot reach the soil, and put landscape fabric or thick mulch under the tree so they cannot burrow in. A yellow sticky trap in mid-spring tells you when the flies arrive so you can spray at the right moment.
seasoned: There is no rescue once maggots are inside the fruit. The backyard controls are sanitation and timing: pick all fruit promptly and completely, gather and destroy dropped cherries so larvae cannot reach the soil, and lay landscape fabric or dense mulch under the tree to block pupation. Yellow sticky traps from mid-spring time any organic spray to a few days after the first fly is caught.

beginner: Cleanup is the main thing: never leave wormy or fallen cherries on the ground, because each maggot that gets into the soil becomes next year's fly. Picking the tree clean every year keeps the numbers down.
seasoned: Sanitation is the backbone: never let infested or dropped fruit sit, since each maggot that reaches the soil is next year's fly. Prompt, complete harvest and a clean orchard floor steadily lower pressure; a single well-picked tree can stay nearly fly-free.

beginner: Ripe cherries that go soft, dimpled, and leaky fast, with tiny white maggots inside, and fruit that ferments and smells sour on the tree. The difference from ordinary fruit flies is that this pest attacks whole, undamaged ripe cherries.
seasoned: Soft, sunken, leaking spots on ripe and ripening fruit, with tiny white larvae inside that collapse the flesh within a day or two; fruit ferments and sours on the tree. Unlike common vinegar flies, this one attacks SOUND, intact ripe fruit.

beginner: A small invasive fly called spotted wing drosophila. Unlike normal fruit flies, the female can cut into whole, healthy ripe cherries to lay her eggs, which hatch into the maggots inside. It multiplies very fast, so it gets worse the longer ripe fruit hangs.
seasoned: Spotted wing drosophila (Drosophila suzukii), an invasive vinegar fly whose females have a saw-like ovipositor that cuts into intact ripe fruit to lay eggs. It builds explosively, completing a generation in as little as a week, so pressure climbs steeply through the harvest window.

beginner: Picking is the control: harvest ripe cherries every couple of days, remove any overripe or fallen fruit, and get the crop into the fridge quickly, since cold stops the maggots. Fine netting and quick, complete picking are the practical home tools.
seasoned: Harvest is the control: pick ripe fruit promptly and completely, remove culls and any overripe or dropped cherries, and refrigerate the crop right away, since cold stops the larvae. Pick every two to three days during ripening. Fine netting and prompt clean-picking are the practical backyard tools; apple-cider-vinegar traps track activity.

beginner: Keep ahead of it by never leaving ripe or rotting cherries on the tree or ground, picking often, and chilling the fruit right away. It uses lots of other plants too, so keeping your whole yard's ripe fruit picked up helps.
seasoned: Lower pressure by never leaving ripe or rotting fruit on the tree or ground, picking on a tight schedule, and chilling fruit immediately. Neighborhood sanitation matters, since the fly uses many wild and garden hosts.

beginner: Clusters of shiny black aphids (tiny soft insects) on the tips of new spring growth, curling and twisting the young leaves, with a sticky coating below that turns black and moldy. It is worst on young trees and mainly stunts new growth rather than ruining fruit.
seasoned: Dense colonies of shiny black aphids on the tips of new spring shoots, tightly curling and twisting the young leaves, with sticky honeydew below that blackens into sooty mold. Heaviest on vigorous young trees; it slows shoot growth but rarely harms fruit directly.

beginner: A small black insect called the black cherry aphid. Its eggs overwinter on the tree and the young hatch to feed on the soft new spring growth. The numbers usually drop on their own by midsummer as the shoots toughen and ladybugs and other helpers move in.
seasoned: The black cherry aphid (Myzus cerasi). It overwinters as eggs on the tree and explodes on the tender spring flush, feeding on sap; populations crash by midsummer as the shoots harden and natural enemies build up.

beginner: Often you can leave it alone, since ladybugs and other helpers clear it by midsummer. On a young tree that is badly hit, blast the colonies off with a hose, or spray the curled tips with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil. Do not over-fertilize, since lush new growth is what the aphids love.
seasoned: Often no action is needed, since beneficials clean it up by midsummer. For a heavy infestation on a young tree, a strong jet of water knocks colonies off, or insecticidal soap or horticultural oil on the curled tips works; protect the ladybugs and lacewings that do most of the control. Avoid high-nitrogen feeding, which fuels the soft growth aphids prefer.

beginner: Avoid heavy feeding that pushes the soft growth aphids love, welcome ladybugs and lacewings, and do not panic over the spring leaf-curl, which usually does not hurt the cherries. A dormant oil spray in late winter cuts down the overwintering eggs.
seasoned: Keep trees vigorous but not over-fed (high nitrogen invites aphids), encourage beneficial insects, and tolerate the early-season curl, which rarely affects the crop. A dormant oil spray reduces overwintering eggs where the pest is chronic.

beginner: Ripe cherries pecked, half-eaten, or gone, sometimes the whole crop in a day or two, with just pits and torn skins left behind. Robins, starlings, waxwings, and jays are the usual culprits and will clean off an unprotected tree.
seasoned: Ripe and ripening cherries pecked, partly eaten, or stripped entirely, often within a day or two of color, with pits and torn skins left on the spurs. Robins, starlings, waxwings, and jays can take the whole crop of an unprotected tree.

beginner: Birds, which zero in on cherries as they ripen. A ripe cherry tree is a magnet, and a flock can clear it faster than any bug. The good news is that a sour cherry is naturally a small tree, so it is much easier to cover than a big sweet cherry.
seasoned: Fruit-eating birds, which key in on cherries as they color. A ripe cherry tree is one of the most attractive food sources in the yard, and a flock can strip it faster than any insect pest. Sour cherry has one built-in advantage: it is naturally small, so it is far easier to net than a full-size sweet cherry.

beginner: Netting is really the only thing that works: cover the whole tree with fine bird netting as the cherries start to color, and tuck it in at the bottom so birds cannot sneak under. A small sour cherry, especially a dwarf like North Star, is easy to cover. Shiny tape and scare balloons help for a little while but birds get used to them.
seasoned: Netting is the only reliable backyard control: drape fine bird netting over the whole canopy as the fruit begins to color, securing it at the bottom so birds cannot get under. A naturally small sour cherry (or a dwarf North Star) is easy to net. Scare devices (reflective tape, balloons) help briefly but birds soon ignore them.

beginner: Plan to net the tree; a sour cherry is small enough to cover easily. Put the net on as soon as the cherries start coloring, not after the birds show up, and tuck it in at the bottom. Nothing else reliably keeps them off.
seasoned: Plan for netting from the start; the small stature of sour cherry makes this easy. Net early, at first color, not after birds have found the tree, and secure the skirt. There is no substitute for physically excluding them.

beginner: Small purple-brown spots on the leaves from late spring, with spots sometimes dropping out to leave little holes. Infected leaves turn yellow and fall, and a bad case strips the tree of leaves by midsummer. This is the most serious sour cherry disease, and Montmorency is hit especially hard, dropping leaves after just a few spots. Losing the leaves early weakens the tree and the crop, this year and next.
seasoned: Small purple-to-brown spots on the upper leaf surface from late spring; the spotted tissue may drop out for a shot-hole look, and infected leaves yellow and fall. It is the single most important disease of sour cherry: Montmorency is highly susceptible and drops leaves after only a few lesions, and heavy infection defoliates the tree by midsummer, which shrinks the crop, leaves fruit soft and poorly ripened, weakens winter hardiness, and cuts next year's bloom.

beginner: A fungus called Blumeriella jaapii. It spends winter in fallen leaves and infects the new leaves during warm, wet spring weather, building up over a wet season until the tree drops its leaves early. Sour cherries, especially Montmorency, catch it easily.
seasoned: The fungus Blumeriella jaapii. It overwinters in fallen leaves and infects new leaves in warm, wet spring and early-summer weather; repeated cycles through a wet season drive the defoliation. Montmorency and most sour cherries are highly susceptible.

beginner: Rake up and destroy the fallen leaves in fall, which is the most useful thing you can do, since the fungus overwinters in them. Keep the tree open so leaves dry fast, and in wet areas an organic-approved spray program starting after the petals fall protects the new leaves. Keeping the leaves on the tree protects both the tree and next year's cherries.
seasoned: Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn to remove the overwintering source, the single most useful home step. Keep the canopy open for fast drying, and in wet regions an organic-approved fungicide program from petal fall through the season protects the new leaves; commercial orchards spray many times a season on Montmorency. Keeping the tree in leaf preserves its hardiness and next year's crop.

beginner: The main thing is raking up and destroying fallen leaves in fall, where the fungus waits out winter. Pruning for good airflow so leaves dry quickly helps too, and a spray program is most important in wet springs and on Montmorency.
seasoned: Autumn leaf cleanup is the backbone, since the fungus overwinters in fallen leaves. Good airflow from pruning and prompt drying after rain reduce infection, and a protective spray program matters most in wet springs and on susceptible Montmorency.

beginner: At bloom, flowers go limp and brown and small gummy dead patches form on the nearby spurs. As cherries ripen, brown spots appear and spread quickly, sometimes rotting a whole fruit in a day or two in warm, wet weather, with a dusty tan fuzz on top. Rotted fruit shrivels into a hard mummy that hangs on. Split cherries rot the fastest.
seasoned: At bloom, infected blossoms wilt and brown and the infection runs into the spur to form a small gummy canker. As fruit ripens, firm brown spots appear and spread fast, rotting a whole cherry within a day or two in warm, wet weather, with a dusty tan spore mass on the surface. Rotted fruit dries into a clinging mummy; cracked fruit is especially vulnerable.

beginner: A fungus called Monilinia. It survives winter in dried mummy fruit and dead twig patches, then releases spores at bloom that infect the flowers, which later cause the fruit to rot. Warm, wet weather makes it spread fast, and a split or wounded cherry rots first.
seasoned: The fungus Monilinia (M. fructicola and M. laxa). It overwinters in mummies and twig cankers; spores at bloom infect flowers, and those infections later seed the fruit rot. Warm, humid, wet weather drives it, and any wound, especially a rain crack, is an open door.

beginner: Cleanup is the main control: take off and destroy every dried mummy from the tree and ground and prune out the gummy dead twig patches, which hold the spores. If bloom is wet, an organic-approved spray at bloom helps protect the flowers. Pick on time, handle gently, throw out any rotting cherry right away, and keep the watering even so fewer split.
seasoned: Sanitation is the core control: remove and destroy every mummy from the tree and ground and prune out gummy twig cankers, since these are the spore sources. In a wet bloom, an organic-approved bloom-time fungicide reduces blossom blight. Pick promptly, handle gently, remove any rotting fruit at once, and keep moisture even so the fruit does not crack.

beginner: Cleaning up all year prevents most of it: never leave dried mummies over winter, prune so the tree is open and the fruit dries fast after rain, pick on time, and keep watering even so the fruit does not split, since split cherries rot first.
seasoned: Year-round sanitation prevents most loss: never leave mummies over winter, keep the canopy open with pruning so fruit dries fast after rain, harvest promptly, and prevent the fruit cracks that invite infection by keeping moisture even.

beginner: Sunken, dark, gummy patches (cankers) on the trunk and branches that ooze amber sap, often killing the branch above them. In spring, flowers and buds may blacken and die, and some buds never open. Sour cherry shrugs it off better than sweet cherry, but it can still kill a young or stressed tree.
seasoned: Sunken, dark, gummy cankers on trunk, scaffolds, and spurs that ooze amber gum, often girdling and killing limbs; in spring, blossoms and spurs blast (blacken and die) and dormant buds fail to open. Sour cherry is somewhat more tolerant than sweet cherry, but canker can still kill a young or stressed tree.

beginner: A bacterium (a microscopic organism) called Pseudomonas syringae. It gets in through wounds, leaf scars, and frost damage during cool, wet weather, and is worse on stressed trees, those in wet soil, hit by frost, or pushed with too much nitrogen.
seasoned: The bacterium Pseudomonas syringae. It infects through wounds, leaf scars, and frost-injured tissue in cool, wet spring and fall weather, and is worsened by anything that stresses the tree: poor drainage, ring nematodes, frost, and high-nitrogen soft growth.

beginner: There is no cure once it sets in. The approach is prevention: cut out the cankered wood well below the dead patch during dry summer weather (not in wet spring), clean your tools between cuts, and pull out a badly infected young tree. Keep the tree healthy and unstressed; copper sprays only help a little.
seasoned: There is no cure once a tree is infected. Management is preventive: cut out cankered wood well below the canker in dry summer weather (not in wet spring), disinfecting tools between cuts, and remove badly infected young trees. Keep the tree unstressed; copper sprays give only partial protection.

beginner: Prevention is everything: plant where the soil drains well, avoid frosty low spots and trunk wounds, paint the trunk white to prevent sunburn cracks, prune only in dry summer weather, and do not over-feed. A healthy, unstressed tree on good ground shrugs it off best.
seasoned: Prevention is everything: plant on well-drained ground, avoid frost-pocket sites and trunk wounds, paint the trunk white against sunscald cracks, prune only in dry summer weather, and never push soft growth with late nitrogen. A vigorous, unstressed, well-drained tree resists it best.

beginner: Water deeply now and then instead of a little every day. Plan on about once or twice a week while a young tree is getting established, easing to about once a week for a fruiting tree in summer heat, adjusting for rain and your soil. The big thing with cherries is to keep the water STEADY: if the soil dries out and then gets a lot of water, the cherries split open. In winter, when the tree is resting, it needs very little and rain usually covers it.
seasoned: Water deep-and-infrequent rather than little-and-often: about once or twice a week while a young tree establishes, easing to roughly weekly for a bearing tree in summer heat, always adjusted for rain and soil. The discipline that matters for cherry is EVEN moisture: a dry-then-wet swing, or rain after a dry spell, drives the fruit to crack. Through winter dormancy water need drops sharply and rainfall usually suffices.

beginner: Each time you water, give a deep soak that reaches all the way down to the roots, not just a splash on top. A young tree wants about 5 gallons per soak. An older, fruiting tree wants roughly an inch of water a week through the season, and more when it is hot. Keeping the water even and steady as the cherries color up is what keeps them from splitting.
seasoned: Water deeply each time so moisture reaches the full root zone, not just the surface. For an establishing tree, on the order of 5 gallons per soak; for a bearing tree, roughly the equivalent of an inch of water per week through the season, more in heat. Steady, deep watering as the fruit colors keeps the cherries from cracking; let the soil swing dry then wet and you invite splitting.

beginner: Water at the ground around the roots with a drip line or soaker hose, and keep the leaves and fruit dry. Spraying water over the top wets the leaves and fruit and helps diseases like brown rot and leaf spot, and water sitting on ripe cherries makes them split, so put the water on the soil, not the tree, and never sprinkle a tree full of ripe cherries.
seasoned: Water at the root zone by drip or soaker and keep the canopy and fruit dry. Overhead watering that wets the leaves and fruit prolongs leaf wetness, feeds brown rot, bacterial canker, and leaf spot, and leaves free water on ripe fruit that drives cracking, so deliver water to the soil, not the tree, and never sprinkle a tree carrying ripe cherries.

beginner: Too much water, or soil that drains poorly, shows up as yellowing leaves, wilting that does not go away even when the soil is wet, and a tree that slowly goes downhill, because the roots cannot breathe. In cherry, soil that stays wet also brings on crown and root rot and the serious disease bacterial canker. Soil that never dries out between waterings is your warning to back off.
seasoned: Overwatering and poor drainage show as yellowing leaves, wilting that persists even in wet soil, and a declining tree, since waterlogged cherry roots suffocate. Chronically wet soil also brings on crown and root rot and predisposes the trunk to bacterial canker, both often fatal. Soil that never dries between waterings is the warning sign to act on.

beginner: Too little water shows as wilting, dull curling leaves, slower growth, and leaves dropping early in a long dry spell. The tricky part with cherries is near harvest: if the tree dries out and then gets rain or a big watering, the nearly ripe cherries split. So keep the water steady and do not let the tree swing from dry to soaked while the fruit is ripening.
seasoned: Underwatering shows as wilting, dull curling leaves, slowed shoot growth, and early leaf drop in a long dry spell. The cruel twist with cherry is at harvest: a tree run dry and then rained on, or deep-watered after drought, splits its nearly ripe fruit. Catch the dry stress before the swing, and keep moisture even through the final swell.

beginner: While the tree is getting established, keep the soil around the roots evenly moist but not soggy. A deep soak of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, more in heat and less after rain, helps the tree grow the deep roots it needs.
seasoned: Through establishment, keep the root ball and surrounding soil consistently moist, never waterlogged. Deep soaks of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, adjusted for rain and heat, build the deep root system the tree relies on later.

beginner: While the cherries are sizing up and coloring, keep the water steady. Aim for about an inch of water a week as deep soaks, and do not let the soil go dry and then soak it. Steady watering now is what keeps the cherries from splitting.
seasoned: As the fruit sizes and colors, keep moisture EVEN. Aim for about an inch of water per week as deep soaks and avoid dry-then-wet swings. This is the window where steady soil moisture is the difference between sound fruit and a cracked crop.

beginner: After the leaves drop and the tree is resting for winter, it needs very little water. Let rain do most of the work and only water during long dry stretches so the roots do not dry out. Do not keep the soil soaked in winter.
seasoned: Once dormant and leafless, water need drops sharply; rely on rainfall and water only in prolonged dry spells so roots do not desiccate. Avoid keeping dormant soil saturated, which invites root rot and canker.

beginner: Give the tree a deep soak now and then rather than a little every day, and water at the ground (a drip line or soaker hose is ideal) instead of spraying the leaves, since wet leaves and fruit lead to disease. With cherries the most important thing is keeping the water even: do not let the soil dry out and then soak it, especially while the fruit is ripening, or the cherries will split.
seasoned: Water deeply and infrequently at the root zone, by drip or soaker, to drive deep rooting; never wet the canopy, which feeds brown rot, leaf spot, and bacterial canker and leaves free water on fruit. The cherry-specific rule is EVEN moisture: keep the soil steady through the final swell, because a dry-then-wet swing or rain on ripe fruit is the main cause of cracking.

beginner: The most important time to keep the watering even is the last 2 to 3 weeks before harvest, while the cherries are coloring and filling out. A swing from dry to wet then, or a rain after a dry spell, splits the fruit. The weeks right after bloom matter too, for setting and sizing the fruit.
seasoned: The make-or-break window is the final swell and color change, the last 2 to 3 weeks before harvest, when even moisture protects against cracking and sizes the fruit. A water-stress swing then, or a rain after a dry spell, splits the crop. The weeks just after bloom matter too for fruit set and size.

beginner: Hardening off (slowly getting an indoor-grown seedling used to the outdoors) does not apply to sour cherry. You plant it bare-root and dormant in late winter or early spring, not as a seedling started inside, so there is no tender young plant to ease outdoors.
seasoned: Hardening off does not apply to sour cherry. It arrives as a dormant, bare-root tree and goes in the ground in late winter to early spring, not raised from a seedling indoors, so there is no tender transplant to acclimate.

beginner: Plant the bare-root tree while it is still dormant (resting, no leaves) in late winter to early spring, before the buds open, once the ground can be dug. Soak the roots in a bucket for an hour or two first. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending them, and set the tree so the graft union (the bumpy joint near the base, if the tree is grafted) sits 2 to 3 inches above the soil. Do not put fertilizer in the hole. Refill with the same soil, water in well, and add a stake only if it is windy. You only need one tree, since sour cherry fruits on its own.
seasoned: Plant the bare-root tree while dormant in late winter to early spring, before bud break, once the ground can be worked. Soak the roots an hour or two beforehand. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending them and set the tree with the graft union (the swollen joint near the base, if the tree is grafted) 2 to 3 inches above the final soil line. Do not fertilize the hole; backfill with native soil, water in well, and stake if the site is windy. No pollinizer is needed, since sour cherry is self-fruitful, so a single tree is all you plant.

beginner: Fill the pot with a chunky, fast-draining mix made for shrubs and trees, not a soft peat-based potting soil that stays soggy. A bark-based mix (composted bark with perlite or pumice for drainage) holds the air the roots need. Do not use yard soil in a pot, since it packs down and drains badly when you water often.
seasoned: Use a coarse, fast-draining soilless mix built for woody plants, not a peat-heavy potting soil. A bark-based mix (composted pine bark with perlite or pumice) gives the air-filled porosity stone-fruit roots demand; cherry will not tolerate a mix that holds water against the crown. Skip native soil in a pot, which compacts under irrigation.

beginner: Keep it simple and aim for drainage. If the mix holds water, stir in more perlite or pumice, and lay a thin layer of compost on top instead of mixing a lot of rich material throughout. Stay away from water-holding crystals or heavy peat, since wet roots rot and invite canker.
seasoned: Keep amendments minimal and drainage-first: blend in extra perlite or pumice if the base mix feels water-retentive, and top-dress with a thin layer of compost rather than mixing heavy organics throughout. Avoid moisture-retentive crystals or large peat fractions, which work against the fast-draining root zone cherry needs.

beginner: A cherry in a pot dries out much faster than one in the ground. In summer heat, check it daily and water when the top inch or two feels dry, until water runs out the bottom, but never let the pot sit in a saucer of water, since wet roots rot. The catch is that cherries crack from uneven watering, so a pot, which swings wet and dry fast, makes cracking more likely, another reason a ground tree is easier. In winter, give just enough to keep the root ball from drying out completely.
seasoned: A potted cherry dries far faster than one in the ground and has no deep soil to buffer it, so check moisture daily in summer heat and water when the top inch or two is dry, until it runs from the drainage holes, but never leave the pot in a full saucer. The hard part is that cherry cracks on uneven moisture and a pot swings wet-to-dry fastest, so consistency is doubly important. Through dormancy, water only enough to keep the root ball from drying completely.

beginner: Watering often washes food out of the pot, so feed a little at a time. Use a diluted balanced liquid fertilizer every few weeks from spring into early summer, then stop, so the tree does not push tender growth that winter cold can damage. Do not fertilize at planting, and stop feeding once the tree drops its leaves.
seasoned: Frequent watering flushes nutrients from a pot, so feed lightly and often: a dilute balanced liquid feed every few weeks through the spring-to-early-summer flush, then stop so no soft growth is pushed into fall. Do not feed at planting, and ease off entirely once the tree goes dormant.
